hero.lede: {gear} amps, cabs and pedals running on the laptop you already own. Plug your guitar into your interface and play — no latency, no cost.
hero.note: Free forever. No account, no cloud, no subscription.
hero.supportSub: One person builds this. Free, for everyone.
tone.h2:
The amp responds
like the real one.
tone.lede: Pick attack, sustain, the way a note compresses when you dig in. OpenRig runs neural captures of the real amp, so the response is the same — with no delay between your hand and the speaker.
captures.lede: A capture pack ships dozens of .nam files — one per gain setting, channel and mic. Everywhere else you open them one at a time. OpenRig reads the whole pack and turns it into knobs: turn Gain and the right capture loads itself.
captures.cap1.h3: Turn a knob, not a list
captures.cap1.p: Move the Gain knob and the matching capture loads underneath. It behaves like the amp, not like a file browser.
captures.cap2.p: Rust DSP built in, neural amp captures, LV2 and VST3 plugins and impulse responses — all five load into the same chain.
captures.cap3.p: Point it at your folder of .nam files or IRs and it builds the same knob panel from them.
rig.lede: No menus, no parameter lists. Pedals, amps and cabs sit in a row like a pedalboard, and the knob you want is where you expect it.
rig.cap1.p: Drag a knob and hear it move. Every control responds the moment you touch it.
rig.cap2.p: Pedals in front, cabs behind, drag anything to reorder it.
rig.cap3.p: Found it? Save the preset. It's still there at soundcheck next month.
band.lede: Guitar, acoustic and a vocal mic at the same time — each with its own chain, its own gear and its own outputs. Nothing bleeds between them.
inst.lede: Pick the instrument and OpenRig shows only the gear that fits it.
inst.i1.p: Amps, cabs, drives, the whole board.
inst.i4.p: A generic rig for whatever the session needs.
inst.note: Bass and keys rigs are next up.
gig.lede: Rehearsal room, living room or a stage with a click in your in-ears — it behaves the same every night.
gig.c1.p: The signal goes out and comes back fast enough that your hands never notice the computer.
gig.c2.p: Change amp, add a pedal or load a preset while you're playing. No gap, no pop, no dead bar.
gig.c3.p: The laptop you already own is the rig. Nothing extra to buy, nothing extra to carry to the gig.
features.lede: Looper, tuner, metronome, spectrum analyzer and a tone diagnosis, all built in. You never leave the app to check or fix the sound.
features.f1.p: Record a take, listen back, record another on top. One take at a time, no undo maze.
features.f2.p: Play a dry DI file through the live chain — every pedal and amp treats it exactly like your guitar. Test a tone without picking up the instrument.
features.f3.p: Tap tempo, time signature, subdivision and its own output. Keeps the whole band in time.
features.f4.p: A chromatic tuner per input, muting the output while you tune.
features.f5.p: Real-time spectrum per input, left and right — you can see what you're playing.
features.f6.p: Points out fizz, mud and boom against a genre reference, and tells you how to fix it.
features.more.presets.p: Your whole board, saved. Call it back from the screen, a footswitch or Claude.
features.more.scenes.p: Verse, chorus, solo. Same rig, one tap between them.
features.more.midi.p: Assign any knob or switch with MIDI Learn. Plug in an M-Vave Chocolate and it comes mapped.
features.more.multi.p: Guitar into one interface, monitors out of another. OpenRig runs both at the same time.
features.more.insert.p: Got one you won't give up? Send the signal out to it and back, mid-chain.
ai.h2:
Ask for the tone.
Claude builds it.
ai.lede: OpenRig speaks MCP. Tell Claude you want the sound off a particular record and it researches the real signal chain, picks the gear from the catalog and saves the preset onto your rig — while you keep playing.
ai.c1.p: Name a song or an artist. It researches the chain that was actually used, maps it to the catalog and saves it as a new preset.
ai.c2.p: Point it at your .nam/IR captures or a tone3000.com pack and it packages a real OpenRig plugin, manifest and all.
ai.c3.p: Describe your footswitch, or hand it a MIDI capture, and it writes the profile — no factory support needed.
ai.skillsText: Six skills, one plugin — see them all on GitHub.
app.lede: Instruments on the left, gear in the middle, outputs on the right. That's the whole app.
app.caption: Every knob, every parameter — one screen.
story.h2:
This started because three
multi-effects units cost a fortune.
story.p1: My son started guitar lessons. His teacher had one sound, we had another one at home, and what he learned in the lesson didn't happen again afterwards. Fixing that by buying everyone the same unit cost more than the instrument.
story.p2: I've been a developer for 26 years. At the time I was investigating, with method, how far you can go programming with AI — and a study like that is only worth anything if the problem is hard. Live audio is hard: the code runs a few hundred times a second and, when it gets it wrong, the sound fails right there, in front of everyone. There's no hiding it.
story.p3: It worked out better than I expected. OpenRig today is a real-time audio platform written in Rust: every input is an isolated runtime, so two guitars on the same interface really are two independent rigs. Amp, cab and pedal mixing native DSP, neural captures and IRs in the same chain. Presets in plain text you can open and edit.
story.p4: And the original idea grew with it: instead of one tone for me and my son, one computer on stage processing the whole band, each musician working on their own sound. Only one of them needs the gear.
road.lede: All of it is public. Each line is an issue on GitHub you can read, comment on or pick up.
road.done.i1: Chain editor with real knobs, drag to reorder
road.done.i2: Five backends in one rig — native, NAM, LV2, VST3, IR
road.done.i3: Capture packs turn into knobs on their own
road.done.i4: Presets and scenes switching without a gap in the sound
road.done.i6: Looper, DI loop, metronome, tuner, spectrum, Tone Doctor
road.done.i7: MCP server and the Claude skills
road.done.i8: Several interfaces at once, insert loop for hardware

fund.lede: OpenRig has no company behind it and nothing to sell you. It stays free and open source either way — money decides how fast it moves and how many machines it runs on.
fund.c1.p: Audio interfaces, footswitches and a Windows and a Linux machine to build and test on. Right now it's whatever is already in the room.
fund.c2.p: Capture packs, licences and studio time to model amps properly instead of guessing.
fund.c3.p: Every hour funded is an hour on the list above.
fund.note: No tiers, no paywalled features, no "pro" version. Ever.
dl.lede: OpenRig is free and open source. Download it, open it and start playing — nothing to sign up for, nothing to unlock later.
